subject: Medical Terminology
title: Lecture 14 and 15 - Blood and Lymphatic System

A.q: Which description of blood's composition is correct?
options: The liquid portion is serum, and the formed cellular portion consists of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.
The liquid portion is lymph, and the formed cellular portion consists of megakaryocytes, fibroblasts, and osteocytes.
The liquid portion is plasma, and the formed cellular portion consists of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.
The liquid portion is plasma, and the formed cellular portion consists of lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets.
A.explain: Blood is a fluid connective tissue whose liquid part is plasma and whose cellular part is erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. Serum is the post-clotting fluid and is not the living liquid matrix of circulating blood. Lymph belongs to the lymphatic system, and megakaryocytes, fibroblasts, and osteocytes are marrow and connective-tissue cells rather than the circulating formed elements. Lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets omit the red cells and the granulocyte class, so that list is not the full cellular composition.

A.q: Which set of duties belongs to the lymphatic system rather than to blood itself?
options: Filtering foreign particles from lymph, sustaining lymphocyte responses, balancing tissue fluid, and absorbing dietary fats
Delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells, conveying hormones to their targets, and removing carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes
Generating the pressure that drives flow, opening and closing its own valves, and perfusing the heart muscle through coronary vessels
Producing red cells, white cells, and platelets, storing calcium salts, and giving attachment to skeletal muscle
A.explain: The lymphatic system filters microorganisms and foreign particles out of lymph, supports lymphocyte activity during immune responses, maintains the internal fluid environment between capillaries and tissue cells, and carries fats away from the digestive system. Delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing carbon dioxide and wastes is the transport work of blood. Generating flow pressure and opening valves describes the heart and its vessels. Producing blood cells, storing minerals, and giving muscle attachment are skeletal and marrow roles.

A.q: Plasma and serum are both liquid fractions of blood. Which statement about them is correct?
options: Serum still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors; plasma is the fluid left once blood has clotted.
Plasma and serum both lack clotting factors and differ only in whether red cells remain suspended in them.
Plasma and serum both hold all the clotting factors and differ only in their content of dissolved proteins.
Plasma still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors; serum is the fluid left once blood has clotted.
A.explain: Plasma still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors. Serum is the fluid left once blood has clotted, without those factors. The other options swap the two or claim they share the same factors.

A.q: Hemoglobin, the pigment within red cells, is best described as which kind of substance?
options: A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to a calcium compound
A storage pigment built from a protein bound to an iron-protein compound
A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to an iron compound
A visual pigment built from a protein bound to a retinal-protein compound
A.explain: Hemoglobin is a respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to an iron compound. A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to a calcium compound names the wrong metal. A storage pigment built from a protein bound to an iron-protein compound names the wrong pigment class. A visual pigment built from a protein bound to a retinal-protein compound is not the red-cell pigment.

A.q: Which statement correctly separates granulocytes from agranulocytes?
options: Granulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules, while agranulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules
Granulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules, while agranulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules
Granulocytes reside in the bone marrow, while agranulocytes reside in the lining of the small intestine
Granulocytes manufacture antibodies, while agranulocytes perform phagocytosis of invading germs
A.explain: Granulocytes are the polymorphonuclear leukocytes whose nuclei show several lobes and whose cytoplasm holds protein granules, namely neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Agranulocytes are the mononuclear leukocytes with one large nucleus, clear cytoplasm, and no granules, namely lymphocytes and monocytes. Granulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules, while agranulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules, swaps the two definitions. Location in marrow versus gut does not define the split. Antibody production belongs to B lymphocytes, and phagocytosis is shared by neutrophils and monocytes, so that assignment misreads the classes.

A.q: A granulocyte that fights infection by phagocytosis and is the most common white cell is which type?
A.explain: The neutrophil is the granulocyte whose cytoplasmic granules take a neutral stain and that clears infection by phagocytosis, with a lifespan of up to about 24 hours. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The basophil stains dark blue. The monocyte also phagocytoses for about a day but is an agranulocyte with no granules.

A.q: Which white cell stains dark blue, takes part in immune surveillance, and releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue?
A.explain: The basophil is the short-lived granulocyte, usually under two days, that stains dark blue, contributes to immune surveillance, and brings anticoagulant substances to inflamed tissues. The neutrophil stains neutral. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The lymphocyte is an agranulocyte active in adaptive immunity.

A.q: Which white cell stains bright yellow-red to orange and increases during parasitic infection and allergic reactions?
A.explain: The eosinophil is the granulocyte that stains bright yellow-red, orange, or rosy and whose count rises during parasitic infections and allergic reactions, with a lifespan of about two to five days. The basophil stains dark blue. The neutrophil stains neutral. The monocyte is a non-granular phagocyte.

A.q: The word polymorphonuclear describes the granulocytes. Which reading of its parts is correct?
options: Poly means many, morpho means form, and nucleus means kernel, so the term refers to the many-lobed nucleus of these cells.
Poly means few, morpho means color, and nucleus means cell, so the term refers to the pale staining of these cells.
Poly means many, morpho means granule, and nucleus means sac, so the term refers to the granular cytoplasm of these cells.
Poly means one, morpho means form, and nucleus means center, so the term refers to the single round nucleus of these cells.
A.explain: In polymorphonuclear, poly means many, morpho means form, and nucleus means kernel, so the word describes the many-lobed nucleus of the granulocytes. Poly means few, morpho means color, and nucleus means cell misglosses the elements. Poly means many, morpho means granule, and nucleus means sac turns morpho into granule. Poly means one, morpho means form, and nucleus means center turns poly into one and describes a mononuclear cell.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells?
A.explain: The T-cell matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells. The B-cell makes antibodies, the NK-cell kills through cytotoxic substances, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte arises in the bone marrow?
A.explain: The B-cell arises in the bone marrow and makes antibodies against antigens. The T-cell matures under thymic influence, the NK-cell kills through cytotoxic substances, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte destroys tumor or infected cells through cytotoxic substances?
A.explain: The NK-cell, or natural killer cell, carries cytotoxic substances that kill tumor or infected cells. The T-cell attacks cells after maturing in the thymus, the B-cell makes antibodies, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: Immunity, as a physiological mechanism, is best defined as the body's ability to do what?
options: Pump oxygen-rich blood to every tissue and return oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
Recognize foreign materials and neutralize or remove them without harming itself
Filter out old and damaged red cells and store the iron freed by their breakdown
Absorb dietary fats from the digestive tract and carry them into the bloodstream
A.explain: Immunity is the set of physiological mechanisms by which the body recognizes a material as foreign and then neutralizes, eliminates, or metabolizes it without injuring its own tissue. Pump oxygenated blood to every tissue while returning deoxygenated blood to the lungs is cardiac circulation. Filter out old and damaged red cells and store the iron recovered from their breakdown is a splenic function. Absorb dietary fats from the digestive tract and return them to the bloodstream is a lymphatic function.

A.q: Which pairing of term to definition is correct?
options: Antigen is a Y-shaped protein that destroys an invader, and antibody is the invader that triggers that protein.
Antigen and antibody are both foreign substances that enter the body from external sources.
Antigen is any substance that provokes antibody formation, and antibody is the Y-shaped protein that inactivates that antigen.
Antigen is the Y-shaped protein made by B cells, and antibody is the cytotoxic substance stored in natural killer cells.
A.explain: An antigen is any substance that, once introduced, causes the body to form antibody against it, and an antibody is the Y-shaped protein the body produces to destroy or inactivate that antigen. Antigen is a Y-shaped protein that destroys an invader, and antibody is the invader that triggers that protein, reverses the two roles. Antigen and antibody are both foreign substances that enter the body from external sources, treats the antibody as a foreign entrant. Antigen is the Y-shaped protein made by B cells, and antibody is the cytotoxic substance stored in natural killer cells, swaps both the shape and the cell of origin.

A.q: Which contrast between active and passive immunity is correct?
options: Active immunity is long-lasting and made by the body itself; passive immunity is short-lasting and received from outside.
Active immunity is short-lived and received from outside; passive immunity is long-lived and made by the body itself.
Active immunity is long-lived but received from outside; passive immunity is short-lived but made by the body itself.
Active and passive immunity are both short-lived and both come from maternal antibodies passed across the placenta.
A.explain: Active immunity is long-lasting because the body makes its own antibodies. Passive immunity is short-lasting because the antibodies are received from outside. The other options swap or mix these features.

A.q: Within active immunity, how do the natural and artificial forms differ?
options: Natural active immunity follows a vaccine, while artificial active follows an infection
Natural active immunity is given as serum, while artificial active passes in breast milk
Both forms are short-lived and depend on antibodies supplied from another person
Natural active immunity follows an infection, while artificial active follows a vaccine
A.explain: Active immunity means the host makes its own antibodies. The natural route is recovery from an actual infection, and the artificial route is vaccination. Natural active immunity follows a vaccine, while artificial active immunity follows a natural infection, swaps the two labels. Natural active immunity is given as antiserum, while artificial active immunity is passed through breast milk, lists transfers of preformed antibody, which are passive. Both natural and artificial active immunity are short-lived and rely on antibodies from another source, calls active immunity short-lived and dependent on an outside source.

A.q: Within passive immunity, how do the natural and artificial forms differ?
options: Natural passive immunity follows a vaccine, while artificial passive follows recovery from infection.
Natural passive immunity passes by placenta and breast milk, while artificial passive is injected serum.
Natural passive immunity is built by the host after exposure, and artificial passive after a vaccine.
Both forms are long-lasting states built by the host’s own memory cells after first contact.
A.explain: Passive immunity supplies preformed antibody. The natural route is maternal transfer across the placenta and through breast milk, and the artificial route is an injection of serum that already contains antibodies. Natural passive immunity follows a vaccine given to the host, while artificial passive immunity follows the host's recovery from a clinical infection, describes active immunity. Natural passive immunity is built by the host after an exposure, while artificial passive immunity is built by the host after a vaccine dose, also describes active immunity. Both natural and artificial passive immunity are long-lasting states created by the host's own memory cells after first contact, gives passive immunity the duration and memory of active immunity.

A.q: Which option lists pairs in which both members of every pair carry the same meaning?
options: Chrom/o with Splen/o; Hem/o with Thromb/o; Thym/o with Immun/o
Chrom/o with Hem/o; Splen/o with Thromb/o; Lymph/o with Immun/o
Chrom/o with Chromat/o; Hem/o with Hemat/o; Thym/o with Thym/i
Chrom/o with Lymph/o; Hem/o with Splen/o; Thromb/o with Thym/o
A.explain: Chrom/o and Chromat/o both mean color, Hem/o and Hemat/o both mean blood, and Thym/o and Thym/i both mean thymus. Chrom/o with Splen/o, Hem/o with Thromb/o, and Thym/o with Immun/o pairs color with spleen, blood with clot, and thymus with safe. Chrom/o with Hem/o, Splen/o with Thromb/o, and Lymph/o with Immun/o pairs color with blood, spleen with clot, and clear fluid with safe. Chrom/o with Lymph/o, Hem/o with Splen/o, and Thromb/o with Thym/o pairs color with clear fluid, blood with spleen, and clot with thymus.

A.q: In the term hemochromatosis, the element chrom refers to what?
A.explain: The term splits into hem/o meaning blood, chrom meaning color, and the suffix -osis meaning a condition, so chrom contributes the sense of color, as in the pigment or iron-color deposits of hemochromatosis. Blood is carried by the hem element of the same word. Clot and spleen belong to thromb/o and splen/o, which do not appear here.

A.q: In the term thrombophlebitis, the element thrombo refers to what?
A.explain: The term joins thrombo meaning clot, phleb meaning vein, and the suffix -itis meaning inflammation, so thrombo contributes the sense of clot. Vein is the phleb element of the same word. Color and blood belong to chrom/o and hem/o, neither of which is present.

A.q: In the term lymphoduct, the element lympho refers to what?
A.explain: Lympho is the combining form for the clear fluid lymph, so in lymphoduct it names that fluid and the term means a duct carrying lymph. Thymus, spleen, and color are the senses of thym/o, splen/o, and chrom/o.

A.q: What does the term hematocytopenia mean?
A.explain: Hematocytopenia is built from Hemat/o (blood), cyt/o (cell), and -penia (deficiency), so it denotes a deficiency of blood cells. An excess would use -osis or -cytosis, a platelet deficiency is thrombocytopenia, and clotting-factor excess is not the sense of this term.

A.q: What does the term splenomegaly mean?
A.explain: Splenomegaly is built from Splen/o (spleen) and -megaly (enlargement), so it denotes an enlarged spleen. Inflammation would use -itis, removal would use -ectomy, and pain would use -dynia.

A.q: What does the term thrombophlebitis mean?
options: Inflammation of an artery caused by a clot
Inflammation of a vein caused by a clot
Hardening of a vein caused by a clot
Surgical removal of a clot from a vein
A.explain: Thrombophlebitis is built from Thromb/o (clot), phleb (vein), and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a vein caused by a clot. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term thymocyte mean?
options: A cell of the bone marrow
A cell of the lymph node
A.explain: Thymocyte is built from Thym/o (thymus) and -cyte (cell), so it denotes a cell of the thymus. Spleen cells would use Splen/o, bone marrow cells would use Myel/o, and lymph node cells would use Lymph/o.

A.q: What does the term athymism mean?
A.explain: Athymism is built from the prefix a- (without), Thym/o (thymus), and -ism (condition), so it denotes the absence of the thymus. Enlargement would use -megaly, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical removal would use -ectomy.

A.q: What does the term immunopharmacology mean?
options: The study of drugs that act on the immune system
The study of immune cells circulating in the blood
The study of the immune response to an infection
The treatment of immune disorders without any drugs
A.explain: Immunopharmacology joins immun/o (safe, immune), pharmac/o (drug), and -logy (study), so it is the study of drugs that act on the immune system. The other options keep the immune sense but drop the drug or study parts.

A.q: What does the term hemochromatosis mean?
options: A condition of excess blood cells
A condition of excessive iron deposits
A condition of deficient blood clotting
A condition of excess clots in the veins
A.explain: Hemochromatosis is built from Hem/o (blood), chromat/o (color), and -osis (condition), so it denotes a condition involving excessive iron deposits and the resulting skin color changes. Excess blood cells would use -cytosis, deficient clotting would use a different suffix, and excess clots in veins is thrombophlebitis.

A.q: Which structure is the lymphoid organ that produces T-lymphocytes to fight off foreign organisms?
A.explain: The thymus produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms. The spleen filters old blood cells, the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix helps house good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease?
A.explain: The spleen filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the bone marrow produces blood cells, and the Peyer's patches monitor and destroy bacteria in the small intestine.

A.q: Which structures trap pathogens from food and air and act as the first line of defense against foreign invaders?
options: The Peyer's patches and lymph nodes
A.explain: The tonsils and adenoid trap pathogens from food and air and act as the first line of defense against foreign invaders. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters blood cells, the bone marrow produces blood cells, the appendix houses good bacteria, and the Peyer's patches monitor bacteria in the small intestine.

A.q: Which structure produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets?
A.explain: The bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens.

A.q: Which structures are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria?
A.explain: The Peyer's patches are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria. The tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure plays a role in housing good bacteria?
A.explain: The appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air.

A.q: Which fluid is the colorless, watery liquid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the bloodstream?
A.explain: Lymph is the colorless, watery fluid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the circulatory system by the lymphatic network. Plasma and serum are blood fractions, and interstitial fluid is the tissue fluid before it enters the lymphatic capillaries.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between interstitial fluid and lymph?
options: Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells, and lymph is that fluid once inside blood capillaries.
Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells, and lymph is that fluid once inside lymphatic capillaries.
Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells, and lymph is that fluid once it leaves nodes for veins.
Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells, and lymph is a separate fluid made in the lymph nodes.
A.explain: Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells; once it enters the lymphatic capillaries it is called lymph. Fluid that enters blood capillaries joins the plasma, lymph is already lymph before it leaves the nodes, and the nodes filter lymph rather than make it.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the function of valves in the lymphatic vessels?
options: They stop lymph from flowing backward toward the tissues.
They contract on their own and push lymph forward like a small pump.
They let lymph flow both ways so that pressure stays balanced.
They close to stop lymph from ever entering the bloodstream.
A.explain: Valves in lymphatic vessels stop lymph from flowing backward, so it keeps moving toward the bloodstream. They do not pump, do not allow two-way flow, and do not block entry into the blood.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the flow of lymph through a lymph node?
options: Lymph enters through the efferent vessel and leaves through the afferent vessel
Lymph enters through the afferent vessel and leaves through the efferent vessel
Lymph enters and leaves through the same afferent vessel of the node
Lymph enters through the thoracic duct and leaves through the right lymphatic duct
A.explain: Lymph enters a lymph node through the afferent lymphatic vessel and leaves through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The other options reverse the two, use one vessel for both, or name the large ducts instead.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes how lymph is returned to the bloodstream?
options: Lymph enters lymphatic capillaries, passes through lymph nodes, and returns to the veins through lymphatic ducts.
Lymph enters lymph nodes, passes into lymphatic capillaries, and returns to the veins through lymphatic ducts.
Lymph enters lymphatic capillaries, passes through lymph nodes, and empties straight into the right atrium.
Lymph enters lymphatic capillaries, passes through lymph nodes, and drains into the hepatic portal vein.
A.explain: Lymph is collected by lymphatic capillaries, filtered as it passes through lymph nodes, and returned to the venous blood through the lymphatic ducts. The other options reverse the order or send lymph to the wrong endpoint.

A.q: Match each type of blood cell to the feature that defines it.

rightItems.text: Granulocyte with neutral-staining granules that phagocytoses pathogens
Cell fragment shed from megakaryocytes that is essential for coagulation
Respiratory carrier of oxygen and carbon dioxide that contains hemoglobin
Granulocyte with dark blue granules that releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue
Agranulocyte with a single large nucleus that phagocytoses germs and infected cells
Granulocyte with orange to rosy granules that rises in parasitic and allergic states

A.explain: The erythrocyte is the respiratory carrier with a lifespan of about 110 to 120 days. The neutrophil is the granulocyte whose granules stain neutral and that phagocytoses pathogens with a lifespan up to about 24 hours. The basophil is the granulocyte with dark blue granules that releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue. The eosinophil is the granulocyte with orange to rosy granules that rises in parasitic and allergic states. The monocyte is the agranulocyte with a single large nucleus that phagocytoses germs. The thrombocyte is the cell fragment shed from megakaryocytes that is essential for coagulation. Each feature is phrased so that the cell must be identified by its granule stain, lifespan, or role rather than by a repeated name.

A.q: Match each type of lymphocyte to the feature that defines it.

rightItems.text: Matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign, cancerous, and virus-infected cells.
Arises in the bone marrow and manufactures antibodies against antigens.
Acts as a natural killer carrying cytotoxic substances that destroy tumor or infected cells.

A.explain: T-cells are thymus-dependent and target foreign, cancerous, and virus-infected cells, living about 30 to 160 days, so they match the thymic-influence feature. B-cells are bone-marrow derived and produce antibodies, living about five to six weeks, so they match the antibody-manufacturing feature. NK-cells are natural killers holding cytotoxic substances that destroy tumor or infected cells, living up to about two weeks, so they match the cytotoxic feature. The three lineages are distinguished by their site of maturation and their effector mechanism, not by granule content, since all are agranulocytes.

A.q: Match each lymphatic organ to the role it performs.

rightItems.text: Generates T-lymphocytes that combat foreign organisms.
Filters out and removes aged or damaged blood cells and fights infection.
Forms red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Traps pathogens from food and air as a first line of defense.
Monitors and destroys bacteria along the small intestine.

A.explain: The thymus produces the T-lymphocytes that fight foreign organisms, the spleen filters and removes old and damaged blood cells while resisting infection, the tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air as a first line of defense, the bone marrow is the source of red cells, white cells, and platelets, the Peyer's patches sit in the wall of the small intestine to monitor and destroy bacteria, and the appendix helps house good bacteria. Each organ is fixed to its own role by what it makes or what it filters, so the pairing follows the function rather than the position in the body.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.
A.explain: Chrom/o and Chromat/o both mean color, as in hemochromatosis, Hem/o and Hemat/o both mean blood, as in hematocytopenia, Splen/o means spleen, as in splenomegaly, Thromb/o means clot, as in thrombophlebitis, Immun/o means safe, as in immunopharmacology, and Lymph/o means the clear fluid lymph, as in lymphoduct. The remaining form of this group, Thym/o with Thym/i, means thymus, as in thymocyte and athymism.

A.q: Match each term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: Inflammation of a vein caused by a clot.

A.explain: Hematocytopenia is a deficiency of blood cells. Splenomegaly is enlargement of the spleen. Thrombophlebitis is inflammation of a vein caused by a clot. Thymocyte is a cell of the thymus. Athymism is absence of the thymus. Each term is built from the combining forms and suffixes of this unit, and the meaning follows directly from those elements.

A.q: Match each blood cell to its lifespan.
A.explain: The erythrocyte lives about 110 to 120 days. The neutrophil and the monocyte both live up to about 24 hours, so they share one answer. The basophil usually lives under 2 days, and the eosinophil about 2 to 5 days. The thrombocyte lives about 7 to 10 days. The T cell lives about 30 to 160 days, the B cell about 5 to 6 weeks, and the NK cell up to about 2 weeks.

A.q: Match each immunity route to how long it lasts.
A.explain: Natural active and artificial active immunity are long-lasting, because the host makes its own antibodies. Natural passive and artificial passive immunity are short-lasting, because the antibodies come from another source.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the lymph nodes in the lymphatic system?
options: They filter microorganisms and foreign particles from lymph passing through.
They collect interstitial fluid from between the tissue cells to form lymph.
They drain lymph from the right side of the head and chest into the blood.
They stop lymph from flowing backward along the length of the vessels.
A.explain: Lymph nodes filter microorganisms and foreign particles from lymph. Collecting interstitial fluid is the job of lymphatic capillaries, draining the right upper body is the right lymphatic duct, and preventing backflow is the job of valves.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of lymphatic capillaries?
options: They filter foreign particles from lymph inside the lymph nodes.
They collect interstitial fluid and begin its return to the blood.
They drain lymph from the left upper body into the left subclavian.
They return lymph straight into the right atrium of the heart.
A.explain: Lymphatic capillaries collect interstitial fluid, which becomes lymph, and begin its return to the blood. Filtering happens in the nodes, the thoracic duct drains the left upper body, and lymph does not go straight to the heart.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the thoracic duct in the lymphatic system?
options: It drains lymph from the lower body and the left upper body into the blood.
It drains lymph from the right side of the head, neck, and chest into the blood.
It drains lymph from the lower body only into the right atrium.
It drains lymph from the left arm only into the lymph nodes.
A.explain: The thoracic duct drains lymph from the lower body and the left upper body into the blood. The right side of the head, neck, and chest drains through the right lymphatic duct.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the right lymphatic duct in the lymphatic system?
options: It collects lymph from the lower body and left upper body and returns it to the blood.
It collects lymph from the right side of the head and chest and returns it to the blood.
It collects lymph from the right arm only and returns it to the lymph nodes.
It collects lymph from both legs and returns it straight to the right atrium.
A.explain: The right lymphatic duct collects lymph from the right side of the head and chest and returns it to the blood. The lower body and left upper body drain through the thoracic duct.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the thymus in the lymphatic system?
options: It produces B-lymphocytes that manufacture antibodies.
It produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms.
It produces red blood cells that carry oxygen.
It produces platelets that are essential for clotting.
A.explain: The thymus produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms. B-lymphocytes, red cells, and platelets come from the bone marrow.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the bone marrow in the lymphatic system?
options: It produces red blood cells and platelets, but no white cells.
It produces white blood cells and antibodies, but no red cells.
It produces lymph, lymphocytes, and antibodies, but no platelets.
It produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
A.explain: The bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Each other option leaves out at least one of these or adds lymph and antibodies, which the marrow does not produce.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the Peyer's patches in the lymphatic system?
options: They monitor and destroy bacteria in the stomach and colon lining.
They monitor and destroy bacteria in the throat tonsils.
They monitor and destroy bacteria in the small intestine lining.
They monitor and destroy old blood cells in the spleen.
A.explain: Peyer's patches sit in the lining of the small intestine, where they monitor and destroy bacteria. The tonsils guard the throat and the spleen removes old blood cells.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the appendix in the lymphatic system?
options: It houses old blood cells until they are removed.
It houses T-lymphocytes until they mature.
It houses good bacteria that support the gut.
It houses lymph until it returns to the veins.
A.explain: The appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria. Old blood cells are removed by the spleen, T-lymphocytes mature in the thymus, and lymph returns to the veins through the lymphatic ducts.

A.q: A formed element that contains hemoglobin and carries oxygen and carbon dioxide is which type?
A.explain: This is the erythrocyte, the red cell that contains hemoglobin and carries the respiratory gases. The leukocyte, thrombocyte, and lymphocyte do other work.

A.q: This white cell is the most common one in the blood and fights infection by phagocytosis. Which is the correct spelling of this cell?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Neutrophil. Neutrophill, Neutrofil, and Neutraphil are misspellings.

A.q: This white cell increases during parasitic infection and allergic reactions. Which is the correct spelling of this cell?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Eosinophil. Eosinophill, Eosinofil, and Eosinaphil are misspellings.

A.q: This white cell takes part in immune surveillance and brings anticoagulants to inflamed tissue. Which is the correct spelling of this cell?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Basophil. Basophill, Basofil, and Basaphil are misspellings.

A.q: A white cell with one large nucleus and no granules that gives rise to three lineages is which type?
A.explain: This is the lymphocyte, the agranulocyte that gives rise to T-cells, B-cells, and NK-cells. The monocyte has no lineages, and the neutrophil and basophil carry granules.

A.q: The largest white cell, with no granules, that destroys germs by phagocytosis, is which type?
A.explain: This is the monocyte. The lymphocyte gives rise to lineages, and the neutrophil and eosinophil carry granules.

A.q: A cell fragment shed by the megakaryocyte that is essential for coagulation is which type?
A.explain: This is the thrombocyte, or platelet. The erythrocyte, leukocyte, and monocyte are whole cells with other jobs.

A.q: Which reading of the parts neutr and phil in neutrophil is correct?
options: A color sense, and a clot
A.explain: Neutr means neither, and phil means attraction for, because the granules take neither an acid nor a basic stain.

A.q: Which three lineages arise from the lymphocyte?
A.explain: The lymphocyte gives rise to the T-cell, the B-cell, and the NK-cell. The other sets mix granulocytes, red cells, and platelets.

A.q: Which nucleus pattern belongs to the lymphocyte?
options: Several nuclear lobes and protein granules
No nucleus, as a cell fragment
One large nucleus and no granules
A pigment mass and no nucleus
A.explain: The lymphocyte has one large nucleus and no granules. Lobed nuclei with granules fit the granulocytes, and the platelet and red cell have no nucleus.

A.q: Which germs does the monocyte destroy by phagocytosis?
options: Bacteria only, not viruses or fungi
Viruses only, not bacteria or fungi
A.explain: The monocyte destroys viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protozoa. Each other option names only part of that list.

A.q: Match each white cell to its class.
A.explain: The neutrophil, eosinophil, and basophil carry granules, so they are granulocytes. The lymphocyte and monocyte lack granules, so they are agranulocytes.

A.q: Match each white cell to how its granules stain.
A.explain: Neutrophil granules stain neutral, eosinophil granules bright yellow-red to orange, and basophil granules dark blue to blue-black. The lymphocyte and monocyte have no granules.

A.q: Where does the T-cell mature?
A.explain: The T-cell matures in the thymus, under thymic influence. The B-cell arises in the bone marrow; the spleen and lymph nodes filter but are not where T-cells mature.

A.q: Where does the B-cell arise?
A.explain: The B-cell arises in the bone marrow. The T-cell matures in the thymus, and the spleen and lymph nodes are filtering organs.

A.q: Which payload does the NK-cell carry?
A.explain: The NK-cell carries cytotoxic substances. Antibodies come from B-cells, neutral granules from neutrophils, and anticoagulants from basophils.

A.q: This lymphoid organ produces the lymphocytes that attack foreign organisms. Which is the correct spelling of this organ?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Thymus. Thymous, Thimys, and Thymuss are misspellings.

A.q: This organ filters out old and damaged blood cells and fights infection. Which is the correct spelling of this organ?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Spleen. Splean, Splene, and Splein are misspellings.

A.q: This structure pairs with the tonsils to trap pathogens from food and air. Which is the correct spelling of this structure?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Adenoid. Adeniod, Adinoid, and Adenoide are misspellings.

A.q: This soft tissue fills the cavities inside bones and is where blood cells form. Which is the correct spelling of this tissue?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Bone marrow. Bone marroww, Bone merrow, and Bone marow are misspellings.

A.q: These structures sit in the lining of the small intestine and monitor bacteria. Which is the correct spelling of these structures?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Peyer's patches. Payer's patches, Peir's patches, and Peyar's patches are misspellings.

A.q: This structure helps house beneficial bacteria. Which is the correct spelling of this structure?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Appendix. Apendix, Appendex, and Appendixs are misspellings.

A.q: Which parent of platelets resides in the bone marrow?
A.explain: The megakaryocyte resides in the bone marrow and sheds platelets. Lymphoblasts, monoblasts, and erythroblasts give rise to other cells.

A.q: Match each combining form to its other accepted spelling.
A.explain: Chrom/o is also written chromat/o, hem/o is also written hemat/o, and thym/o is also written thym/i.

A.q: Which real term uses Chrom/o?
A.explain: The real term is Hemochromatosis. Hematocytopenia uses hemat/o and cyt/o, not chrom/o. Chromocytopenia and Chromatophlebitis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Hem/o?
A.explain: The real term is Hematocytopenia. Hemoductosis, Hematosplenitis, and Hemothymism are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Splen/o?
A.explain: The real term is Splenomegaly. Splenoductosis, Splenothymism, and Splenochromatosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Thromb/o?
A.explain: The real term is Thrombophlebitis. Thrombochromia, Thrombosplenism, and Thromboductosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Immun/o?
A.explain: The real term is Immunopharmacology. Immunochromatosis, Immunoductosis, and Immunosplenism are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Lymph/o?
A.explain: The real term is Lymphoduct. Lymphochromia, Lymphothymism, and Lymphosplenosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses the prefix for absence with Thym/o?
A.explain: The real term is Athymism. Athymocytosis, Athymoduct, and Athymochromia are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which formed element is named for its role in clotting?
A.explain: The thrombocyte shares the clot sense of thromb/o. The erythrocyte, lymphocyte, and monocyte use other forms.

A.q: Match each immunity route to the event that produces it.

rightItems.text: Transfer by placenta and breast milk

A.explain: Natural active immunity follows recovery after an infection, and artificial active immunity follows a vaccine. Natural passive immunity comes by placenta and breast milk, and artificial passive immunity by injected antibody-containing serum.

A.q: Which set of findings belongs to hemochromatosis?
options: Iron deposits, yellow skin, and spleen enlargement
Excess red cells, bronze skin, and vein clots
Fat deposits, bronze skin, and liver cirrhosis
Iron deposits, bronze skin, and liver cirrhosis
A.explain: Hemochromatosis deposits excess iron in the tissues, giving bronze skin pigmentation and cirrhosis of the liver. Each other set swaps in one wrong finding.

A.q: What does RBC stand for?
A.explain: RBC stands for red blood cell. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does WBC stand for?
A.explain: WBC stands for white blood cell. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does NK stand for?
A.explain: NK stands for natural killer. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does SCT stand for?
A.explain: SCT stands for specialized connective tissue. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: Which two classes divide the white blood cells?
A.explain: White blood cells divide into granulocytes and agranulocytes. Erythrocytes and thrombocytes are not white cells, and B-cells, T-cells, monocytes, and lymphocytes all belong to the agranulocytes.

A.q: Which lifespan belongs to the red blood cell?
A.explain: The red blood cell lives about 110 to 120 days. About 60 to 80 days and about 70 to 90 days fall short of it, and about 2 to 5 days fits the eosinophil.

A.q: Which other name belongs to the red blood cell?
A.explain: The red blood cell is also called the erythrocyte. Leukocyte, thrombocyte, and lymphocyte name other cells.

A.q: Which other name belongs to the white blood cell?
A.explain: The white blood cell is also called the leukocyte. Erythrocyte, thrombocyte, and megakaryocyte name other elements.

A.q: Match each fluid to its description.

rightItems.text: Clear yellowish blood fraction that still holds clotting factors
Liquid left after clotting, without clotting factors
Fluid that bathes tissue cells outside the vessels
Colorless watery liquid inside the lymphatic vessels

A.explain: Plasma still holds the clotting factors, and serum is what remains after clotting. Interstitial fluid bathes the tissue cells and is called lymph once it enters a lymphatic capillary.

A.q: Which loads does plasma carry besides clotting factors?
options: Lymph, bile, and suspended blood cells
Water and cells, but no proteins
A.explain: Plasma carries water, proteins, and suspended cells. Lymph and bile are not plasma loads, and plasma carries both water and proteins.

A.q: This term names an inherited disorder seen in blood and lymph work-ups. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?
Which tissue changes belong to Hemochromatosis?
options: Bronze skin pigmentation and liver cirrhosis
Bronze skin pigmentation and spleen fibrosis
Yellow skin pigmentation and liver cirrhosis
Pale skin pigmentation and marrow failure
Hem/o, chrom, and a condition ending
Hem/o, chrom, and an inflammation ending
Hemat/o, chrom, and a condition ending
Hem/o, chromat/o, and a tumor ending

A.explain: This term is hemochromatosis. Hemochromotosis, Hemachromatosis, and Hemochromatasis miss the spelling. Iron overload deposits produce bronze skin pigmentation and can cirrhose the liver. Vein redness and clot after catheter injury fits thrombophlebitis, enlargement of the spleen after congestion is splenomegaly, and absence of the thymus from early life is athymism. The elements are hem/o, chrom, and a condition ending. An inflammation ending would make it an inflammation, hemat/o is not the blood form used in this term, and a tumor ending would name a growth.

A.q: This term appears when blood test results are reported. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Hemat/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending
Hemat/o, cyt/o, and an excess ending
Hem/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending
Hemat/o, cyst/o, and a deficiency ending

A.explain: This term is hematocytopenia. Hematocytopenya, Hemotocytopenia, and Hematocitopenia miss the spelling. It means a deficiency of blood cells. An excess of blood cells reverses the ending. A deficiency of platelets only would use thromb/o. An excess of clotting factors is not this term. The elements are hemat/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending. An excess ending reverses the meaning, hem/o is not the blood form used in this term, and cyst/o means bladder or sac, not cell.

A.q: This term is used when an abdominal organ is examined. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Splen/o, megal/o, and a condition ending

A.explain: This term is splenomegaly. Splenomegally, Spleenomegaly, and Splenomegaaly miss the spelling. It means enlargement of the spleen. Inflammation of the spleen, removal of the spleen, and absence of the spleen use other endings. The elements are splen/o and an enlargement ending. An inflammation ending or a removal ending names a different change, and splen/o with megal/o and a condition ending is a wrong split.

A.q: This term names a problem found in a limb after a long period of immobility. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Inflammation of a vein associated with a clot
Inflammation of an artery associated with a clot
Inflammation of the spleen associated with a clot
Enlargement of a vein associated with a clot
Thromb/o, phleb, and an inflammation ending
Thromb/o, phleb, and an enlargement ending
Thromb/o, arteri, and an inflammation ending
Thrombocyt/o, phleb, and an inflammation ending

A.explain: This term is thrombophlebitis. Thromboflebitis, Thrombophlebittis, and Thrombophlebitus miss the spelling. It means inflammation of a vein associated with a clot, including clot and redness after vein trauma. Inflammation of an artery associated with a clot would use arteri/o. Inflammation of the spleen associated with a clot would use splen/o. Enlargement of a vein associated with a clot uses an enlargement ending, not -itis. The elements are thromb/o, phleb, and an inflammation ending. An enlargement ending names swelling, arteri names an artery, and thrombocyt/o names the platelet rather than the clot.

A.q: This term names a field of study within the immune topics. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: The study of drugs that act on the immune system
The study of immune cells circulating in the blood
The study of the immune response to an infection
The treatment of immune disorders without any drugs
Immun/o, pharmac/o, and a study ending
Immun/o, pharmac/o, and a disease ending
Immun/o, pharmac, and a drug ending
Imm/o, pharmac/o, and a study ending

A.explain: This term is immunopharmacology. Immunofarmacology, Immunopharmocology, and Immunopharmacollogy miss the spelling. It means the study of drugs that act on the immune system. The study of drugs that act on the heart, the kidneys, or the lungs would use other organ forms. The elements are immun/o, pharmac/o, and a study ending. A disease ending names a disorder, a heart-only study needs a heart form, and imm/o is a wrong split of immun/o.

A.q: This term names a cell found in an immune organ. Answer each step, then the next term follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: A cell of the lymph node

A.explain: This term is thymocyte. Thymosyte, Thimocyte, and Thymocyt miss the spelling. It means a cell of the thymus. A cell of the spleen would use splen/o, a cell of the marrow would use a marrow element, and a cell of the lymph node would use lymph/o. The elements are thym/o and a cell ending. A tumor ending names a growth, thyr/o names the thyroid, and an enlargement ending names swelling.

A.q: This term names an immune problem present from early life. Answer each step, then the immunity run follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: A-, thym, and a condition ending
A-, thym, and an inflammation ending
Ana-, thym, and a condition ending
A-, thyr, and a condition ending

A.explain: This term is athymism. Athymisim, Athymysm, and Athymasm miss the spelling. It means absence of the thymus. Enlargement of the thymus would use -megaly, inflammation of the thymus would use -itis, and a cell of the thymus is thymocyte. The elements are a- for without, thym, and a condition ending. An inflammation ending names inflammation, ana- means up or again, and thyr names the thyroid.
